newsitem.title: UK: Police limit last march of N.Ireland season.
newsitem.headline: Police limit last march of N.Ireland season.

text.p: Police on Tuesday banned parts of the last set-piece parade of Northern Ireland's turbulent marching season after Catholics, flexing new-found muscle, objected to the route.
The province, torn apart by Catholic riots over a Protestant parade a month ago, awaited word from Catholics in Londonderry on whether the police ban met their demands.

Catholic residents of Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city, had planned massive counter-demonstrations for when the Apprentice Boys, a Protestant order, hold their annual march around the city's ancient walls on Saturday.
They wanted so-called feeder parades, which join the main march from outlying villages and towns, banned because they pass through Catholic areas whose residents say they are sectarian intimidation.

Police said that feeder parades through the villages of Dunloy, Bellaghy and the Lower Ormeau Road of Belfast, had all been banned, clearing the way for Londonderry residents to allow Saturday's march by thousands of Protestants.
They awaited formal word from the Bogside Residents' Association, which represents Catholics in the overwhelmingly Irish nationalist city of Londonderry, that the new route was acceptable.
This year's marching season exploded into violence on July 6 when police allowed the Protestant Orange Order to hold a march through the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown.

Riots erupted nightly, forcing Britain to reinforce its Northern Ireland army, but peace was restored when the Orange Order decided to scrap its most contentious parades on July 12, after police said they could guarantee their safety.

Saturday's parade is of symbolic importance to Protestant activists. It commemorates a 1689 siege of Londonderry by a Catholic monarch which was thwarted when Apprentice Boys - trainees - slammed the gates of the city shut.

Part of the march is along the old walls of the city overlooking the Catholic Bogside area, where civil rights marches in 1969 erupted into a political and sectarian conflict that became known as "The Troubles".

Last year the parade was postponed after another violent marching season, and a 200-metre stretch of the walls directly above the low-cost housing estate was sealed off to avoid giving offence when it was finally permitted in October.

The decision on feeder parades was announced on the eve of the first formal talks between Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, and Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, in Belfast.

Adams, whose Catholic-backed organisation wants an end to British rule of Northern Ireland, has campaigned for years to get Protestant parades banned or re-routed to avoid offending the minority population.

Mowlam and Adams will discuss arrangements for resumed multi-party peace talks, which Sinn Fein will be allowed to join if a July 20 truce by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas is deemed genuine by Mowlam and her security advisers.

The talks are under a cloud because the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), the main voice of the pro-British Protestant majority, wants the IRA to pledge that it will disarm and disband to prove that its truce is genuine.

But Britain and Ireland, which co-sponsor the talks, say that guerrillas should be allowed to disarm in stages as the talks progress. The UUP says this will effectively allow Sinn Fein to negotiate with a secret army at its back.
